text.p: The aluminum fundamentals justify the current rally in aluminum market, which reached a 21-month high on the London Metal Exchange Friday, producers and analysts said.

While many traders have noted the collapse of the cash-to-three-month contango and the November-December spread raises the possibility of a squeeze, producers point to the sharp decline in London Metal Exchange stocks and buoyant demand as evidence that higher prices were long overdue.

"In the summer, industrial activity normally slows due to vacation schedules," wrote the often-bullish analyst Stuart Spector, in his monthly report. "(But) this year, the world economy remained buoyant and aluminum bookings were strong. Thus, there is a need for more metal units when end-users come back to work and crank up their production schedules."
"The fundamentals have been good for quite some time," said one Midwest producer. "We're surprised that the price hasn't moved up sooner."
He noted that London Metal Exchange warehouse stocks have declined 343,100 tonnes, or 35.4 percent, to 626,750 tonnes since Jan. 16.

Some dealers say the decline is the result of moving metal off of LME warrant without actually moving the metal out of the warehouse. But the producer disagreed. "The bulk of that decline is consumption."

"The narrowing in the forward contango and not the backwardation in forward contracts makes it impossible for merchants to finance cash and carry positions," Spector said. "Thus, the ingot moving out of the LME warehouses is for real consumption."
"Demand has been excellent," another producer said. "If the level of business is any indication, it's no surprise we're at 80 cents a pound."
The London Metal Exchange three-month price was $1,738 a tonne, while the cash price was $1,743 a tonne (79.06 cents a lb).
The Midwest premium was 4.00-5.00 cents over LME cash, dealers said.
